issues.legal_issue: The rule of frustration applies to an agreement to create a lease, but not to a completed lease.
material_facts: The parties agreed to a lease for three years, which could be validly created only by a registered instrument.
No lease deed was executed or registered.
issues.conclusion: There was only an agreement to lease, not a completed lease, so the agreement fell within the scope of the law of frustration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Contract Act applies to contracts, including an executory agreement to lease, but does not invalidate a completed transfer. Once a valid lease comes into existence, the agreement to lease is replaced by the lease. The Court relied on Raja Dhruv Dev Chand v. Harmohinder Singh.

rule.if: lease_transaction and registration_required_for_term and not registered_instrument

predicates.lease_transaction: The parties have made an arrangement for one party to take property on lease from another.
predicates.registration_required_for_term: The agreed lease term requires a registered instrument for the lease to be validly created.
predicates.registered_instrument: The parties executed and registered an instrument creating the lease.

issues.definition: When a lease arrangement requires registration but no instrument creating the lease is registered, the arrangement remains an executory agreement to which the law of frustration applies.

issues.legal_issue: A supervening event makes performance impossible when it renders performance impracticable or useless in light of the parties’ purpose and strikes at the basis of the contract.
material_facts: The agreement contemplated that the lessees would enjoy the properties by cultivating them or sub-leasing them.
Communal disturbances and the subsequent circumstances made it impossible for the lessees to reach the properties, take possession, cultivate them, or collect rent from the cultivators.
The lessees were not responsible for the circumstances preventing performance.
The agreement did not require the lessor to deliver actual possession; the lessees were responsible for obtaining possession after registration.
issues.conclusion: The supervening circumstances made the agreement impossible to perform, and the Court upheld the finding that it had become frustrated.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 56 of the Contract Act, impossibility is not limited to physical or human impossibility. Performance that becomes impracticable or useless in light of the parties’ object and purpose is impossible where the supervening event takes away the basis of the contract and strikes at its root. The Court relied on Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur and Co.

rule.if: contract_dispute and executory_agreement and supervening_event_unpreventable and performance_impracticable and event_strikes_contract_basis

predicates.contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a contractual obligation remains enforceable after a later event.
predicates.executory_agreement: The parties have an agreement whose promised performance has not been completed as a transfer or other completed transaction.
predicates.supervening_event_unpreventable: An event occurring after the agreement, which the promisor could not prevent, obstructs performance.
predicates.performance_impracticable: The event makes performance impracticable or useless in light of the purpose for which the parties made the agreement.
predicates.event_strikes_contract_basis: The event takes away the basis of the agreement and strikes at its root.

issues.definition: When an unpreventable event after an executory agreement makes performance impracticable in light of the parties’ purpose and strikes at the agreement’s basis, the agreement is discharged for supervening impossibility.
